THOUGHT: This 61-year-old female presents with a classic triad for Plummer–Vinson syndrome (PVS): dysphagia (due to an upper esophageal web), iron deficiency anemia (Hb 10 g/dL, koilonychia, glossitis, pale conjunctivae), and fatigue. The unintentional weight loss is likely secondary to chronic dysphagia leading to reduced oral intake. Mild anterior neck pain may reflect localized inflammation or tissue changes associated with the web or underlying mucosal atrophy. The barium esophagram confirming an upper esophageal web is a hallmark radiographic finding in PVS. Laboratory findings support iron deficiency: microcytic anemia (though MCV not provided, koilonychia + glossitis + low Hb are highly specific), and the elevated WBC (11,000/mm³) with normal ESR (10 mm/hr) suggests no acute infection or systemic inflammation — consistent with chronic nutritional deficiency rather than malignancy or autoimmune disease. While esophageal webs can occur in other conditions (e.g., GERD, graft-versus-host disease), the constellation of iron deficiency stigmata (glossitis, koilonychia, pallor), dysphagia, female sex, and age align strongly with PVS. Importantly, PVS is associated with an increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma of the hypopharynx and esophagus, so this diagnosis carries both therapeutic and surveillance implications. Other considerations — such as thyroiditis (neck pain, fatigue, weight loss) — are less likely given absence of goiter, lymphadenopathy, or abnormal thyroid function tests (not provided but notably absent from workup), and no signs of hyper- or hypothyroidism. Esophageal malignancy would typically present with progressive dysphagia (often to solids then liquids), but the presence of a benign-appearing web on barium study and lack of alarm features (e.g., stridor, hematemesis, severe weight loss >10% body weight, lymphadenopathy) makes malignancy less likely as the primary diagnosis — though it remains a critical concern requiring endoscopic evaluation and biopsy per guidelines.

DIAGNOSIS: Plummer–Vinson syndrome
